choices: Structs are always slower than classes — convert Point to a class
The method receives a copy of the struct; mutations affect only the copy — pass by ref, return the modified struct, or use a class
Value types can't have methods — remove Move from the struct
The compiler caches struct field writes — add volatile to dx
scenarios.hint: `Point` is a struct. When you pass a struct to a method, what does the method receive — the original or something else?
scenarios.prompt: Why didn't the point move?
scenarios.situation: A Move method mutates a Point struct's fields, but the caller's point is unchanged.
scenarios.title: The point that wouldn't move
scenarios.why: Structs are value types: passing one to a method copies the entire value, so mutations hit the copy. Fixes: pass with ref/out, return the modified struct, or model it as a class (reference type) when identity and mutation matter. This is the fundamental value-vs-reference distinction — small immutable data (coordinates, money) suits structs; entities with identity suit classes.

choices: Enable nullable reference types and declare the field as string? — the compiler then warns on dereference without a null check
Wrap every access in try/catch NullReferenceException — exceptions are the null-handling mechanism
Initialize all strings to string.Empty — null strings are illegal in C#
Disable warnings CS8600-CS8604 — they slow down compilation
scenarios.hint: C# 8 added a compile-time feature that makes 'this reference might be null' part of the type. What annotation marks a maybe-null string?
scenarios.prompt: How should the code express and guard the nullability?
scenarios.situation: A DisplayName field is sometimes null and crashes with NullReferenceException.
scenarios.title: The null display name
scenarios.why: Nullable reference types (string? vs string) move nullability into the type system: the compiler warns when you dereference a maybe-null reference without checking. Declaring string? DisplayName documents the reality and forces callers to handle it (null check, ?. operator, or throw). try/catch for nulls and blanket string.Empty initialization hide the domain meaning of 'no display name'.

choices: async void is the recommended return type for all async methods — the crash is elsewhere
The loop is fine — Task.Delay doesn't actually yield in console apps
Await each download (or collect the tasks and await Task.WhenAll) — fire-and-forget tasks let Main exit and unobserved exceptions crash the process
Replace await with .Result — blocking is safer than awaiting
scenarios.hint: The tasks are started but never awaited. What happens to Main — and to an exception thrown in a task nobody observes?
scenarios.prompt: What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: Downloads start but the program prints 'done' immediately and exits; some downloads never finish.
scenarios.title: The downloads that never finished
scenarios.why: Unawaited tasks are fire-and-forget: Main doesn't wait for them, and exceptions in unobserved tasks surface unpredictably (or crash the process). Awaiting each call — or gathering tasks and awaiting Task.WhenAll for concurrency — makes completion and errors part of the control flow. (async void is only for event handlers; it can't be awaited and crashes on exceptions.)

choices: var results = query.ToList() at the start — materialize early to avoid multiple enumeration
The query executes on each enumeration (deferred execution) — materialize once with ToList() if enumerated multiple times, or restructure to enumerate once
LINQ queries cache their results automatically after the first enumeration
Replace Where with a for loop — LINQ can't be enumerated twice
scenarios.hint: When does a LINQ query actually execute — when it's defined, or when it's consumed? What happens on the second consumption?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the database get hit twice?
scenarios.situation: A LINQ query over orders is counted then enumerated; the database query runs twice.
scenarios.title: The query that ran twice
scenarios.why: LINQ uses deferred execution: the query is just a definition until enumerated, and each enumeration re-executes it. Count() then foreach = two executions (two DB round-trips). Materialize once with ToList()/ToArray() when you need multiple passes, or restructure to a single enumeration. Deferred execution is powerful (composable queries) but demands awareness of when work happens.

choices: Use a record: record Person(string Name, int Age) — records get value-based equality, so two instances with the same data are equal
Override GetHashCode only — Equals follows automatically
Records are reference types with reference equality — use a struct instead
Compare with == after casting both to object — that forces value comparison
scenarios.hint: Classes compare by reference by default. Which C# type gives you value-based equality for data carriers without hand-writing Equals?
scenarios.prompt: How should Person be declared?
scenarios.situation: Two Person objects with identical data compare unequal; the domain needs value equality.
scenarios.title: Equal data, unequal objects
scenarios.why: Records are reference types with value-based equality synthesized by the compiler (Equals, GetHashCode, == all compare member values) — ideal for immutable data carriers like DTOs. A plain class uses reference equality unless you override Equals/GetHashCode by hand. (Records also give with-expressions for non-destructive mutation: a with { Age = 37 }.)

choices: using blocks are only for file I/O — database connections are managed by the pool
Wrap the connection in a using declaration (using var conn = ...) so Dispose runs deterministically even on exceptions
Call conn.Close() at the end of the method — that's sufficient
The garbage collector disposes connections automatically — no action needed
scenarios.hint: What guarantees cleanup runs when an exception takes the happy path away — a manual Close() at the bottom, or a construct the compiler wraps in try/finally?
scenarios.prompt: How should the connection lifetime be managed?
scenarios.situation: A SqlConnection leaks when an exception occurs mid-method.
scenarios.title: The connection that leaked
scenarios.why: IDisposable resources need deterministic cleanup: using var conn = ... compiles to try/finally with Dispose() in the finally, so the connection returns to the pool even on exceptions. A manual Close() at the method's end is skipped when an exception throws. The GC eventually finalizes, but 'eventually' exhausts the connection pool under load — deterministic disposal is the rule.

choices: Make the method static — static methods dispatch dynamically
Mark the method virtual in the base and override in the derived class — virtual enables runtime dispatch; without it the base implementation always runs
Use the new keyword in the derived class — new gives polymorphic behavior
Polymorphism requires interfaces; base classes can't do it
scenarios.hint: The call goes through a `Shape` reference. What determines which implementation runs — the reference type or the object type — and what keyword switches it?
scenarios.prompt: Why does it print 'a shape', and how do you get polymorphic behavior?
scenarios.situation: A derived class method doesn't get called through a base-class reference.
scenarios.title: The circle described as a shape
scenarios.why: Without virtual, method calls bind at compile time to the reference type — Shape.Describe always runs. Marking the base method virtual and the derived one override switches to runtime dispatch on the actual object type. (The new keyword merely hides the base method and keeps static binding — a common source of 'it compiles but calls the wrong one.')

choices: Program to the interface: depend on IMessageSender, inject the implementation — the caller is decoupled from SmtpSender and testable
Depend on the concrete SmtpSender — interfaces add indirection with no benefit
Use a static class for sending — statics are the simplest abstraction
Interfaces can't be constructor-injected — use property injection
scenarios.hint: What can't you do with `new SmtpSender()` inside the class — substitute a fake in a test? Which design lets the caller supply the sender?
scenarios.prompt: How should the dependency be structured?
scenarios.situation: A notifier hard-codes SmtpSender; unit tests would need a real mail server.
scenarios.title: The untestable notifier
scenarios.why: Depending on the IMessageSender abstraction (constructor-injected) inverts the dependency: Notifier no longer chooses or constructs its sender, so tests inject a fake and production wires the real SmtpSender via DI. new-ing the concrete class inside couples the caller to construction details and makes substitution impossible — the core of the Dependency Inversion Principle.

choices: var top = products.OrderBy(p => p.Price).Take(3) — cheapest first
var top = products.OrderByDescending(p => p.Price).Take(3).ToList() — sort descending, take three, materialize
var top = products.Take(3).OrderByDescending(p => p.Price) — take then sort is faster
var top = products.Where(p => p.Price == products.Max(x => x.Price)) — filter by the max
evidence: // TODO: names of the 3 most expensive products
scenarios.hint: Order of operations matters: do you want the top 3 of the sorted list, or the sorted top 3 of the first 3?
scenarios.prompt: Which query is correct?
scenarios.situation: The three most expensive product names are needed from an in-memory list.
scenarios.title: Top three, correctly
scenarios.why: OrderByDescending(p => p.Price).Take(3) sorts first, then takes — the true top 3. Take(3) before sorting takes three arbitrary items then sorts those (wrong answer). The Where/Max variant returns all ties for first place, not three items. Operator order in LINQ is semantics, not style.

choices: First() — it throws a clear exception when empty, which is what you want
FirstOrDefault() with a null check (or SingleOrDefault when exactly one is expected) — choose based on what empty/invalid means for the domain
Last() — the most recently added user is the right default
ElementAt(0) — index access is faster than First()
evidence:
var user = users.First(u => u.Email == email);
// throws InvalidOperationException when the email isn't found
scenarios.hint: `First` throws on empty. Is 'email not found' an exceptional situation here, or an expected outcome the code should handle?
scenarios.prompt: Which operator fits, and why?
scenarios.situation: A login lookup throws InvalidOperationException for unknown emails instead of showing 'user not found'.
scenarios.title: The login that threw
scenarios.why: First() asserts existence — right when empty is a bug, wrong when empty is a normal outcome like 'unknown email'. FirstOrDefault() returns null (or default) for the expected-missing case, letting the code branch to 'user not found'. SingleOrDefault() additionally asserts at most one match. The choice encodes domain knowledge: is absence exceptional or routine?

choices: Mark the class sealed — sealing prevents further derivation while the base stays extensible
Make all methods private — private methods can't be overridden
Sealed is only for structs — classes can't be sealed
Remove the base class — inheritance is the problem
evidence:
class PaymentProcessor { public virtual void Process() { ... } }
// requirements: no one may derive from PaymentProcessor ever again
scenarios.hint: Which keyword on the class declaration closes the inheritance chain?
scenarios.prompt: How do you forbid derivation?
scenarios.situation: A payment processor's behavior must not be altered by subclassing.
scenarios.title: Closing the inheritance chain
scenarios.why: sealed on the class forbids all derivation — the type hierarchy ends there. (sealed on an override method stops further overriding of that method while the class stays extensible.) It's a deliberate API design statement: this behavior is final. Frameworks seal types whose invariants subclassing could break.

choices: Nested foreach loops — LINQ can't group
products.GroupBy(p => p.Category).Select(g => new { Category = g.Key, Count = g.Count(), Avg = g.Average(p => p.Price) }) — group, then aggregate each group
products.Select(p => p.Category).Distinct() then loop — group manually
OrderBy then take the first of each category — sorting groups implicitly
evidence: // TODO: per-category product count and average price
scenarios.hint: You need rows bucketed by category, then one summary row per bucket. Which operator buckets — and what does each bucket give you?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic query?
scenarios.situation: Per-category counts and average prices are needed from a product list.
scenarios.title: Summarize by category
scenarios.why: GroupBy(p => p.Category) buckets elements by key; each IGrouping<string, Product> exposes Key and the group's elements for Count()/Average()/etc. in a single pass. Manual distinct-then-loop re-scans the list per category (O(n·k)); sorting doesn't group. GroupBy is the declarative 'GROUP BY' of LINQ.

choices: app.MapGet("/health", () => "ok") — minimal APIs can't return plain strings
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args); var app = builder.Build(); app.MapGet("/health", () => Results.Ok()); app.Run(); — the four-line minimal API
Minimal APIs require a controller class — MapGet doesn't exist
Use app.UseEndpoints — MapGet was removed in .NET 8
evidence: // TODO: minimal API with GET /health returning 200
scenarios.hint: Minimal APIs need only a builder, Build(), a route mapping, and Run(). What does MapGet map — a path to what?
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimal working Program.cs?
scenarios.situation: A health-check microservice needs GET /health with the least ceremony.
scenarios.title: The four-line API
scenarios.why: Minimal APIs collapse the host setup: CreateBuilder configures DI/logging/config, Build() creates the app, MapGet maps a path to a handler delegate, Run() starts Kestrel. No Startup class, no controller — ideal for small services. Results.Ok()/Results.NotFound() give typed HTTP results when you need more than a plain return value.

choices: UseAuthentication must come before UseRouting, and UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication — auth order is fixed
The pipeline order must be UseRouting → UseAuthentication → UseAuthorization (→ endpoints); authentication establishes identity before authorization checks it
Order doesn't matter — the framework sorts middleware by type automatically
UseAuthorization must come first so anonymous requests are rejected early
scenarios.hint: Authorization answers 'is this identity allowed?' — what must be established before that question can be asked?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the pipeline order?
scenarios.situation: Authenticated users get 401/403 on protected endpoints despite valid tokens.
scenarios.title: Authorization before authentication
scenarios.why: Middleware runs in registration order: UseAuthentication builds the ClaimsPrincipal from the token/cookie; UseAuthorization then evaluates policies against that identity. Reversed, authorization runs with no identity established and rejects everything. The canonical order — Routing → Authentication → Authorization → Endpoints — reflects the logical dependency: route, identify, permit, execute.

choices: AddScoped in a Singleton is fine — the container promotes the scope automatically
Register the processor as Scoped too, or resolve it per-scope via IServiceScopeFactory — a Singleton must not capture a shorter-lived Scoped dependency
Change the repository to Singleton — longer lifetimes are always safe
Disable scope validation — it's a development-only warning
scenarios.hint: The singleton lives forever; the scoped repository lives per-request. What happens to the 'per-request' instance held by the forever object?
scenarios.prompt: What is the lifetime mismatch, and how do you fix it?
scenarios.situation: A singleton service depends on a scoped repository; the app throws at runtime.
scenarios.title: The singleton that captured a scope
scenarios.why: A Singleton holding a Scoped dependency 'captures' it: the per-request repository becomes effectively singleton — stale DbContext, concurrency bugs, disposed-object errors. The container's scope validation catches this in development. Fixes: make the consumer Scoped (or Transient), or inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work. Lifetime rule: a service may only depend on equal or longer lifetimes.

choices: [HttpGet("{id}")] with int id — route values are strings by default and can't be constrained
Use the route constraint [HttpGet("{id:int}")] — constraints reject non-integers with a 404 before the action runs
Parse and validate manually inside the action — constraints don't exist in ASP.NET Core
Return 400 manually — 404 for bad ids is wrong
scenarios.hint: The route template can declare what `{id}` must look like. What suffix restricts it to integers — and what status results when it doesn't match?
scenarios.prompt: How should the route enforce the integer id?
scenarios.situation: /api/orders/abc reaches the action instead of 404ing.
scenarios.title: The id that wasn't an integer
scenarios.why: Route constraints ({id:int}, {id:guid}, {name:minlength(3)}) are part of route matching: non-matching URLs don't match the route at all, yielding 404 without entering the action. Manual parsing inside the action reinvents matching and returns the wrong status family. Constraints keep URL shape rules declarative and co-located with the route.

choices: Return the entity directly — ASP.NET Core wraps everything in 201 automatically
Return CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = order.Id }, order) — 201 with a Location header pointing at the new resource
Return Ok(order) — 200 is fine for creation
Redirect to the GET endpoint — creation should end in a redirect
scenarios.hint: 201 Created pairs with a header telling the client where the new resource lives. Which result type sets both?
scenarios.prompt: What should the POST return?
scenarios.situation: A create endpoint returns 200; the API contract requires 201 with a Location header.
scenarios.title: The creation without a location
scenarios.why: CreatedAtAction (or CreatedAtRoute) returns 201 with the Location header set to the new resource's GET URL — the HTTP contract for creation, enabling clients to fetch what they just created. Returning Ok() misstates the semantics; caches and client libraries treat 201 + Location as 'here's your new resource'. [ApiController] also gives automatic 400s for model-validation failures.

choices: Read configuration via IConfiguration / IOptions<T> injected through DI — testable and environment-aware
Read Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable directly in the service — simplest
Hardcode the connection string per environment with #if DEBUG directives
Store secrets in appsettings.json and commit it — the repo is private
scenarios.hint: The connection string differs per environment and is a secret. What ASP.NET Core abstraction delivers config to a service without hardcoding?
scenarios.prompt: How should the service get its connection string?
scenarios.situation: A service hardcodes its connection string; staging and prod need different values.
scenarios.title: The hardcoded connection string
scenarios.why: IConfiguration (or the typed IOptions<T> pattern) flows appsettings.json, environment-specific files, env vars, and secret stores into services through DI — one build, many environments, no secrets in source. Hardcoding or #if directives fork behavior per build; committed secrets in appsettings.json leak to every clone. The options pattern additionally gives strongly-typed, validated config.

choices: dotnet build — migrations are compiled into the assembly automatically
dotnet ef migrations add AddStatus then dotnet ef database update — the CLI scaffolds the migration and applies it; review the generated code first
Edit the database by hand — the CLI is only for initial creation
Delete the Migrations folder and re-scaffold — cleanest for every change
scenarios.hint: Two CLI verbs: one writes the migration from the model diff, one applies pending migrations to the database. Which order?
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct commands?
scenarios.situation: A new entity property needs to reach the database schema.
scenarios.title: The property without a column
scenarios.why: dotnet ef migrations add scaffolds a migration from the model-vs-snapshot diff (Up/Down methods to review — never blind-apply), and dotnet ef database update applies pending migrations. The snapshot (ModelSnapshot) is what makes the diff work; deleting the folder destroys the history it tracks. Hand-editing the DB desyncs the model from reality.

choices: var orders = _db.Orders.ToList() then loop accessing o.Customer — lazy loading will fetch each customer
var orders = _db.Orders.Include(o => o.Customer).ToList() — eager-load the navigation in the same query
Set LazyLoadingEnabled = true globally — lazy is always the right default
Project with Select after ToList — projection fixes N+1 automatically
scenarios.hint: Each `o.Customer` access fires a query. Which method tells EF to JOIN the related data into the original query?
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the N+1?
scenarios.situation: Listing orders with customer names fires one query per order.
scenarios.title: The Include that was missing
scenarios.why: Navigation properties load lazily (or not at all) by default; touching o.Customer per row issues N queries. Include(o => o.Customer) eager-loads via JOIN in the single initial query. ThenInclude chains deeper levels. The decision is per query — eager where you know you'll need the data, not a global switch.

choices: Add .AsNoTracking() to the read query — tracking is overhead when you never modify the entities
Tracking is free — leave it on for all queries
AsNoTracking prevents the query from executing — use it only with ToList
Disable change tracking globally in OnConfiguring — tracking is never needed
evidence:
// read-only product catalog, 50k rows, high traffic
var products = _db.Products.Where(p => p.Active).ToList();
scenarios.hint: Change tracking snapshots every entity for SaveChanges diffing. For a read-only list, what does that snapshot buy you — and what does it cost?
scenarios.prompt: What is the optimization for this read-only query?
scenarios.situation: A high-traffic read-only catalog query is slower than expected.
scenarios.title: Tracking what you'll never change
scenarios.why: EF Core's change tracker snapshots each materialized entity to detect modifications for SaveChanges — pure overhead for read-only queries (memory + CPU). AsNoTracking() skips it, measurably speeding large read lists. Keep tracking where you intend to modify and SaveChanges; the default is correct for unit-of-work writes, wasteful for read models.

choices: Catch DbUpdateException and retry in a loop — concurrency is handled by retries
Add a [Timestamp] row-version property and handle DbUpdateConcurrencyException — optimistic concurrency detects the lost update
Lock the table for the whole operation — pessimistic locking is the only safe approach
Concurrency can't happen with EF Core — the change tracker serializes access
scenarios.hint: Both requests read quantity=1, both subtract, both save. What database mechanism detects 'the row changed since I read it'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you prevent the oversell?
scenarios.situation: Two concurrent checkouts both read quantity 1 and both succeed, overselling stock.
scenarios.title: The item sold twice
scenarios.why: This is a lost update: read-modify-write without concurrency control. A [Timestamp]/IsRowVersion column makes EF add the original version to the UPDATE's WHERE clause; a concurrent modification changes the version, the update affects 0 rows, and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException for the loser to handle (retry, merge, or reject). Retrying blindly without the token just races again.

choices: var order = _db.Orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == id) — the general query path
var order = _db.Orders.Find(id) — Find checks the change tracker first, avoiding a DB round-trip for already-loaded entities
Find only works on strings — use it for name lookups
They are identical — Find is just an alias
scenarios.hint: The entity is already tracked after the first load. Which method consults the tracker before querying?
scenarios.prompt: Which lookup avoids the redundant round-trip?
scenarios.situation: The same order is fetched twice per request; the second query is redundant.
scenarios.title: The order fetched twice
scenarios.why: Find(key) checks the change tracker first and returns the already-materialized entity without a database hit; FirstOrDefault always queries. Find only works on primary keys — that's its contract and its limitation. Within a request's DbContext lifetime, repeated key lookups via Find are the efficient pattern.

choices: Configure the relationship in OnModelCreating with HasOne/WithMany/HasForeignKey — explicit configuration documents the mapping and controls delete behavior
EF can't map that relationship — use Dapper instead
Conventions handle everything — configuration is never needed
Put the foreign key in the database only — the model doesn't need navigation properties
scenarios.hint: Conventions infer a lot, but cascade delete behavior and the exact FK deserve to be explicit. Where does EF's fluent configuration live?
scenarios.prompt: How should the relationship be configured?
scenarios.situation: An Order-Customer relationship relies purely on conventions; delete behavior is unclear.
scenarios.title: The relationship by convention
scenarios.why: OnModelCreating's fluent API (HasOne(o => o.Customer).WithMany(c => c.Orders).HasForeignKey(o => o.CustomerId).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict)) makes the relationship, FK, and delete behavior explicit and reviewable. Conventions guess — sometimes wrongly — and silent cascade deletes are a data-loss footgun. Explicit mapping is documentation the compiler checks.

choices: [Fact] with three separate test methods — one per case, no sharing
A single [Theory] with [InlineData] rows for each case — one test body, many data rows
One [Fact] with a loop over the cases — loops are simpler than attributes
Skip the cases that pass — only test the failing one
scenarios.hint: You have one behavior and many input/output pairs. Which xUnit feature runs the same body once per data row?
scenarios.prompt: Which xUnit feature fits?
scenarios.situation: A discount function needs the same assertion across many input tiers.
scenarios.title: One test, many cases
scenarios.why: [Theory] with [InlineData] (or [MemberData]/[ClassData] for complex cases) runs the test body once per data row, with each row reported independently — a failure names its row. Copy-pasted [Fact]s drift apart; loops hide which case failed. Theories express 'this property holds for all these examples' directly.

choices: Create a Mock<IEmailSender>, Setup the Send method, pass mock.Object, then Verify the call happened with the right address
Write a FakeEmailSender class by hand for every test — mocks are unreliable
Don't test the notifier — email sending can't be unit tested
Make Send static so tests can call it directly
evidence:
// Notifier depends on IEmailSender
// TODO: verify Notify sends to the right address without a mail server
scenarios.hint: Moq can stand in for the interface. What three steps — arrange the double, act, then what — prove the interaction?
scenarios.prompt: How do you test the interaction?
scenarios.situation: A notifier test must prove the right email address was used, with no mail server.
scenarios.title: Proving the email was 'sent'
scenarios.why: Moq's triple — new Mock<IEmailSender>(), Setup(...) to stub behavior, .Object to inject, then mock.Verify(x => x.Send(expectedAddress, ...)) — tests the interaction contract without infrastructure. Hand-rolled fakes are fine too, but Moq removes the boilerplate. The key: the test doubles the seam (the interface), not the implementation.

choices: Mock the controller's dependencies with Moq and call the action directly — fastest
Use WebApplicationFactory<Program> with an HttpClient — exercises routing, middleware, DI, and filters end-to-end in memory
Start the app manually and test with curl — automation is overkill
Integration tests are impossible in .NET — test layers separately
evidence: // TODO: POST /api/orders through the real pipeline, no network
scenarios.hint: You want the real middleware pipeline and routing but no sockets. What test host boots your actual Program in memory?
scenarios.prompt: How should the API be integration-tested?
scenarios.situation: An orders API needs end-to-end tests through middleware, routing, and DI — without deploying.
scenarios.title: The pipeline, in memory
scenarios.why: WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> boots the real app (your Program's pipeline, DI container, filters) in-process and hands you an HttpClient — true integration tests with no network. Swap real dependencies (e.g., the DbContext) via ConfigureWebHost for test doubles. Direct action calls skip routing/middleware; manual curl isn't repeatable.

choices: Assert the mock repository was called — the mock interaction is the behavior
Seed an in-memory (or Testcontainers) database, call the service, assert the returned data and resulting state — test outcomes, not doubles
Check that SaveChanges was called exactly once — persistence mechanics are the contract
Only test the happy path — error paths are covered by the compiler
evidence:
// OrderService depends on IOrderRepository (mocked)
// current test: repoMock.Verify(r => r.Add(It.IsAny<Order>()))
scenarios.hint: The test verifies the double, not the service. If you deleted the mock, what would the test assert about — the data that comes back?
scenarios.prompt: What is the better assertion strategy?
scenarios.situation: A service test only verifies a mock was called; it wouldn't catch wrong calculations.
scenarios.title: Testing the mock
scenarios.why: Over-mocked tests assert on the test's own scaffolding. Prefer testing observable outcomes: seed data, invoke the service, assert returned values and resulting state. Verify interactions only where the interaction IS the contract (e.g., 'an email was sent'). In-memory EF providers or Testcontainers give a real-enough seam for repository-backed services.

choices: Name it Clearly_States_ExpectedBehavior and assert one behavior — a failing test should tell you what broke without opening it
Name tests Test1, Test2 — the runner numbers them
Put all assertions for the class in one test — fewer tests run faster
Test names don't matter — only the code matters
scenarios.hint: When this test fails at 2 AM, what does its name tell you? What would a name describing the expected behavior tell you?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this test?
scenarios.situation: A test named Test1 with 40 lines and 6 asserts fails; nobody knows what broke.
scenarios.title: The test named Test1
scenarios.why: A test's name is its failure message: ApplyDiscount_VipTier_ReducesTotalBy20Percent tells you what broke before you open the file. One behavior per test keeps failures precise; 40-line multi-assert tests fail ambiguously. Naming is a test-design tool, not cosmetics.

choices: Set a 30-second timeout on every test — timeouts fix flakiness
Quarantine and fix the root cause (shared state, timing assumptions, test-order dependence) — flaky tests erode trust in the whole suite
Delete flaky tests — a smaller green suite beats a larger red one
Re-run the suite until it passes — CI retries are the fix
evidence:
# same commit: green, red, green across three CI runs
# suspect: static cache shared between tests
scenarios.hint: The outcomes vary with nothing changing in the code. What differs between runs — shared mutable state, clocks, ordering?
scenarios.prompt: How should the team handle the flakiness?
scenarios.situation: The suite passes and fails on the same commit; a static cache shared between tests is suspected.
scenarios.title: The test that flips a coin
scenarios.why: Flaky tests (shared static state, DateTime.Now assumptions, parallel-test interference, order dependence) teach developers to ignore red builds — the suite's value collapses. The fix is root-cause: isolate state per test (fresh fixtures, no statics), freeze clocks, avoid timing assertions. Quarantine the offender while fixing; never normalize 'just re-run'.

choices: dotnet build — build output is the deployment artifact
dotnet publish -c Release — produces the self-contained deployable output (assemblies, deps, config) for the target
Copy the source .cs files to the server — the server compiles on first request
dotnet run -c Release on the server — run is the production host
evidence:
$ dotnet publish -c Release -o ./publish
# what does this produce, and why not just build?
scenarios.hint: `build` produces binaries for development; what does `publish` add — runtime deps, trimmed output, a runnable layout?
scenarios.prompt: Why publish instead of build for deployment?
scenarios.situation: A deploy pipeline copies build output; the app fails on the server with missing dependencies.
scenarios.title: Build output on the server
scenarios.why: dotnet build produces intermediate binaries assuming the SDK/tooling context; dotnet publish assembles the complete runnable deployment — app assemblies, NuGet dependencies, runtime config, static assets — into one folder. Framework-dependent publish needs the .NET runtime on the server; --self-contained bundles it. Deploying build output ships an incomplete app.

choices: Set ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production and keep secrets in environment variables or a vault — appsettings.Production.json overlays base settings without committing secrets
Commit appsettings.Production.json with the real secrets — the repo is private
Use #if PRODUCTION in code to switch connection strings
One appsettings.json for all environments — simplicity wins
scenarios.hint: The same build deploys to dev, staging, and prod. Where do the per-environment differences live so the artifact stays identical?
scenarios.prompt: How should per-environment config and secrets be handled?
scenarios.situation: Connection strings differ per environment; secrets are currently in the committed settings file.
scenarios.title: Config per environment
scenarios.why: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT selects the overlay (appsettings.Production.json merges over appsettings.json); secrets come from environment variables or a vault provider, never committed. One build, many environments — the twelve-factor pattern. #if directives fork the binary per environment; committed secrets leak to every clone.

choices: Kestrel is development-only — production requires IIS
Kestrel is the built-in cross-platform server; production typically runs it behind a reverse proxy (nginx/IIS/YARP) for TLS, hardening, and static files
ASP.NET Core apps can't listen on sockets directly — they need IIS
Use dotnet run as the production server — it wraps Kestrel properly
evidence:
var app = builder.Build();
app.Run();  // what serves HTTP here?
scenarios.hint: `app.Run()` starts a server — which one ships inside ASP.NET Core itself?
scenarios.prompt: What serves HTTP in production, and what sits in front of it?
scenarios.situation: The team debates what actually serves traffic when app.Run() executes.
scenarios.title: What serves the traffic?
scenarios.why: Kestrel is the cross-platform web server built into ASP.NET Core — app.Run() starts it. In production it typically sits behind a reverse proxy handling TLS termination, request filtering, and static files (defense in depth; Kestrel alone is fine but the proxy adds hardening). dotnet run is a development command, not a production host.

choices: dotnet add reference — packages are project references
dotnet add package Dapper --version 2.1.35 — restores from NuGet into the package cache; versions are pinned in the csproj
Download the DLL and commit it to lib/ — NuGet is optional
Edit packages.config by hand — that's the modern flow
scenarios.hint: Where do .NET dependencies come from — and what records the exact version so restores are reproducible?
scenarios.prompt: What does the command do, and where is the version pinned?
scenarios.situation: A developer needs to add a NuGet package reproducibly.
scenarios.title: Adding a dependency
scenarios.why: dotnet add package fetches from the NuGet feed into the local package cache and pins the version in the .csproj (<PackageReference>); dotnet restore reproduces it anywhere. Committing DLLs or hand-editing legacy packages.config fights the SDK-style project system. Pinned versions + lock files (when enabled) make restores deterministic.

choices: dotnet watch run — rebuilds and restarts on file changes, keeping the inner loop tight
Manually stop, rebuild, and restart after every change — safest
Edit the DLLs directly — faster than recompiling
dotnet watch is only for Blazor — console apps can't use it
evidence:
$ dotnet watch run
# change a file -> app restarts automatically
scenarios.hint: The inner loop is edit → build → run → test. Which command collapses the middle steps?
scenarios.prompt: What is the tight inner-loop command?
scenarios.situation: A developer restarts the app manually after every change.
scenarios.title: The manual restart loop
scenarios.why: dotnet watch run observes file changes and rebuilds/restarts automatically (with hot reload for supported edits, applying changes without a full restart). The manual stop-build-run cycle wastes minutes per hour; watch collapses it. It's for any project type, not just Blazor.

choices: Debug builds are fine — the JIT optimizes at runtime anyway
Publish with -c Release — Release enables compiler optimizations and strips debug overhead; Debug is for development
Release mode is only for obfuscation — performance is identical
Build configuration doesn't matter — Kestrel decides performance
scenarios.hint: What does the Debug configuration add that production doesn't want — and what does Release enable?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with deploying the Debug build?
scenarios.situation: The deployed artifact was published with -c Debug.
scenarios.title: Debug in production
scenarios.why: Debug configuration disables optimizations, emits full debug symbols, and enables debug-only code paths — slower and heavier. Release enables JIT/code optimizations and is the supported production configuration. The flag is a build contract: develop and diagnose in Debug, ship Release.

lessons.title: C# Language — Core concepts
concepts: Value types: structs are value types: passing one to a method copies the entire value, so mutations hit the copy. Records are reference types with value-based equality synthesized by the compiler (Equals, GetHashCode, == all compare member values) — ideal for immutable data carriers like DTOs.
Struct semantics: fixes: pass with ref/out, return the modified struct, or model it as a class (reference type) when identity and mutation matter.

Nullable reference types (string? vs string) move nullability into the type system: the compiler warns when you dereference a maybe-null reference without checking. A plain class uses reference equality unless you override Equals/GetHashCode by hand.

Null safety: displayName documents the reality and forces callers to handle it (null check, ?. operator, or throw). try/catch for nulls and blanket string.Empty initialization hide the domain meaning of 'no display name'.
Task: unawaited tasks are fire-and-forget: Main doesn't wait for them, and exceptions in unobserved tasks surface unpredictably (or crash the process).

example.walkthrough: LINQ uses deferred execution: the query is just a definition until enumerated, and each enumeration re-executes it. Count() then foreach = two executions (two DB round-trips). Materialize once with ToList()/ToArray() when you need multiple passes, or restructure to a single enumeration.

pitfalls: Common trap: records are reference types with reference equality.
Common trap: LINQ queries cache their results automatically after the first enumeration.
Common trap: the compiler caches struct field writes.
Common trap: using blocks are only for file I/O.

lessons.title: OOP & LINQ — Core concepts
concepts: Dependency inversion: depending on the IMessageSender abstraction (constructor-injected) inverts the dependency: Notifier no longer chooses or constructs its sender, so tests inject a fake and production wires the real SmtpSender via DI. new-ing the concrete class inside couples the caller to construction details and makes substitution impossible — the core of the Dependency Inversion Principle.
LINQ operators: operator order in LINQ is semantics, not style.
Principle: without virtual, method calls bind at compile time to the reference type — Shape.Describe always runs.

example.code:
var user = users.First(u => u.Email == email);
// throws InvalidOperationException when the email isn't found
example.walkthrough: First() asserts existence — right when empty is a bug, wrong when empty is a normal outcome like 'unknown email'. FirstOrDefault() returns null (or default) for the expected-missing case, letting the code branch to 'user not found'. SingleOrDefault() additionally asserts at most one match.

pitfalls: Common trap: polymorphism requires interfaces; base classes can't do it.
Common trap: var top = products.OrderByDescending(p => p.Price).Take(3).ToList().
Common trap: var top = products.Where(p => p.Price == products.Max(x => x.Price)).
Common trap: use the new keyword in the derived class.

lessons.title: ASP.NET Core — Core concepts
concepts: Minimal APIs collapse the host setup: CreateBuilder configures DI/logging/config, Build() creates the app, MapGet maps a path to a handler delegate, Run() starts Kestrel.
Middleware runs in registration order: UseAuthentication builds the ClaimsPrincipal from the token/cookie; UseAuthorization then evaluates policies against that identity.

Captive dependency: the canonical order — Routing → Authentication → Authorization → Endpoints — reflects the logical dependency: route, identify, permit, execute. A Singleton holding a Scoped dependency 'captures' it: the per-request repository becomes effectively singleton — stale DbContext, concurrency bugs, disposed-object errors.

example.walkthrough: IConfiguration (or the typed IOptions<T> pattern) flows appsettings.json, environment-specific files, env vars, and secret stores into services through DI — one build, many environments, no secrets in source. Hardcoding or #if directives fork behavior per build; committed secrets in appsettings.json leak to every clone. The options pattern additionally gives strongly-typed, validated config.

pitfalls: Common trap: minimal APIs require a controller class.
Common trap: ASP.NET Core wraps everything in 201 automatically.
Common trap: the pipeline order must be UseRouting → UseAuthentication → UseAuthorization (→ endpoints); authentication establishes identity before authorization checks it.
Common trap: the framework sorts middleware by type automatically.

lessons.title: Entity Framework — Core concepts
concepts: Migrations: dotnet ef migrations add scaffolds a migration from the model-vs-snapshot diff (Up/Down methods to review — never blind-apply), and dotnet ef database update applies pending migrations.
Eager loading: the decision is per query — eager where you know you'll need the data, not a global switch.
Include(o => o.Customer) eager-loads via JOIN in the single initial query.

Change tracking: find(key) checks the change tracker first and returns the already-materialized entity without a database hit; FirstOrDefault always queries. EF Core's change tracker snapshots each materialized entity to detect modifications for SaveChanges — pure overhead for read-only queries (memory + CPU).
AsNoTracking() skips it, measurably speeding large read lists.

example.code:
// read-only product catalog, 50k rows, high traffic
var products = _db.Products.Where(p => p.Active).ToList();
example.walkthrough: EF Core's change tracker snapshots each materialized entity to detect modifications for SaveChanges — pure overhead for read-only queries (memory + CPU). Keep tracking where you intend to modify and SaveChanges; the default is correct for unit-of-work writes, wasteful for read models.

pitfalls: Common trap: disable change tracking globally in OnConfiguring.
Common trap: delete the Migrations folder and re-scaffold.
Common trap: asNoTracking prevents the query from executing.
Common trap: var orders = _db.Orders.ToList() then loop accessing o.Customer.

lessons.title: Testing — Core concepts
concepts: Theory: [Theory] with [InlineData] (or [MemberData]/[ClassData] for complex cases) runs the test body once per data row, with each row reported independently — a failure names its row.
Moq's triple — new Mock<IEmailSender>(), Setup(...) to stub behavior, .Object to inject, then mock.Verify(x => x.Send(expectedAddress, ...)) — tests the interaction contract without infrastructure.
Interaction testing: prefer testing observable outcomes: seed data, invoke the service, assert returned values and resulting state.

Integration testing: webApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> boots the real app (your Program's pipeline, DI container, filters) in-process and hands you an HttpClient — true integration tests with no network.

example.code:
// Notifier depends on IEmailSender
// TODO: verify Notify sends to the right address without a mail server
example.walkthrough: Moq's triple — new Mock<IEmailSender>(), Setup(...) to stub behavior, .Object to inject, then mock.Verify(x => x.Send(expectedAddress, ...)) — tests the interaction contract without infrastructure. Hand-rolled fakes are fine too, but Moq removes the boilerplate. The key: the test doubles the seam (the interface), not the implementation.

pitfalls: Common trap: integration tests are impossible in .NET.
Common trap: mock the controller's dependencies with Moq and call the action directly.
Common trap: write a FakeEmailSender class by hand for every test.
Common trap: make Send static so tests can call it directly.

concepts: Dotnet build produces intermediate binaries assuming the SDK/tooling context; dotnet publish assembles the complete runnable deployment — app assemblies, NuGet dependencies, runtime config, static assets — into one folder.
Environments: one build, many environments — the twelve-factor pattern. #if directives fork the binary per environment; committed secrets leak to every clone.
Configuration: debug configuration disables optimizations, emits full debug symbols, and enables debug-only code paths — slower and heavier.

Kestrel: in production it typically sits behind a reverse proxy handling TLS termination, request filtering, and static files (defense in depth; Kestrel alone is fine but the proxy adds hardening). dotnet run is a development command, not a production host.

example.code:

app.Run();  // what serves HTTP here?

In production it typically sits behind a reverse proxy handling TLS termination, request filtering, and static files (defense in depth; Kestrel alone is fine but the proxy adds hardening). dotnet run is a development command, not a production host.

Common trap: kestrel is the built-in cross-platform server; production typically runs it behind a reverse proxy (nginx/IIS/YARP) for TLS, hardening, and static files.

lessons.title: C# / .NET — Core concepts
concepts: async/await is about freeing threads, not creating them. Await the Task to unwrap its result; never block on .Result in request code, and use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code that does not need the caller's context.

DI lifetimes are a contract: singleton lives with the app, scoped lives per request, transient per injection. A longer-lived component must never hold a shorter-lived one — use a scope or context factory instead.

LINQ queries are descriptions until materialized. Everything before ToList()/FirstAsync() becomes SQL; everything after runs in memory. Filter, project, and page before materialization or you ship whole tables over the wire.

EF Core tracks entities for change detection — great for updates, wasteful for read-only lists. Use AsNoTracking() for pure reads, and keep migrations as the single source of truth for schema evolution.

Minimal APIs and controllers share the same pipeline: explicit results (Results.NotFound(), Results.Ok()) beat thrown exceptions for control flow, and validation belongs at the boundary before business logic runs.
Nullability is a design tool. Nullable reference types plus explicit null checks at trust boundaries (like Find returning null) turn runtime NullReferenceExceptions into compile-time conversations.

example.walkthrough: The Where/OrderBy/Take chain stays IQueryable, so EF Core translates it to one SQL query with WHERE, ORDER BY, and TOP — only 50 rows cross the network. AsNoTracking skips change-tracking overhead for this read-only list.

pitfalls: Common trap: returning a Task instead of awaiting it — the response serializes the task object, not the data.
Common trap: injecting a scoped DbContext into a singleton — it throws at startup (or worse, silently shares a stale context); use IServiceScopeFactory.
Common trap: ToList() before Where() — materializes the whole table, then filters in memory; keep predicates in the IQueryable chain.
Common trap: blocking on .Result/.Wait() in web code — the classic synchronization-context deadlock; stay async all the way down.

simulations.title: First() on empty
simulations.brief: A LINQ query crashes with InvalidOperationException: 'Sequence contains no elements' — but only for new customers.

steps.symptom: Crash on new-customer accounts; existing customers work fine.
evidence:
var latest = invoices
    .Where(i => i.CustomerId == id)
    .OrderByDescending(i => i.Date)
    .First();  // line 44
options: Read line 44: First() throws when the filtered sequence is empty — new customers have no invoices
steps.explain: First() is a contract: it promises an element exists. New customers have zero invoices, so the promise breaks.

options: Use FirstOrDefault() and handle the null (no invoices yet)
Seed a fake invoice for new customers
steps.explain: FirstOrDefault() models 'maybe empty' honestly; the null then forces the 'no invoices yet' branch to exist — which the business logic needs anyway.

steps.symptom: Fix applied. Verify the behavior contract.
options: Confirm a new customer returns 0 and an existing customer returns their real total
steps.explain: Verify both branches of the new contract: empty → 0, non-empty → the real total.

simulations.debrief: First() asserts non-emptiness; FirstOrDefault() admits it. Pick the operator that matches reality, then handle the empty case explicitly.

simulations.title: Middleware pipeline order
simulations.brief: Restore the order of the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline.

steps.context: Arrange the middleware in the order requests pass through it.
items: Exception handler (catches downstream failures)
Static files (short-circuits for files)
Routing (selects the endpoint)
Authentication & authorization
Endpoint execution (the controller)

simulations.debrief: Exception handling wraps everything; static files short-circuit early; routing, auth, then the endpoint. Order is behavior in middleware pipelines.

simulations.title: Quarantine or fix?
simulations.brief: A test fails intermittently in CI but passes locally. Decide how to handle it.

steps.text: The test fails ~1 in 20 CI runs, always passes locally. First move?

choices.label: Quarantine it (mark explicit/skip with a tracking issue) so the suite stays trustworthy while you investigate
choices.feedback: Right: a flaky test poisons the whole suite's signal. Quarantine first, investigate second.

choices.label: Rerun until green and merge
choices.feedback: Rerunning until green trains the team to ignore red builds.

choices.label: Delete the test — it was probably wrong
choices.feedback: Deleting a test deletes coverage of whatever it was checking.

steps.text: Quarantined. The failure correlates with parallel test execution. Root cause hypothesis?

choices.label: Shared mutable state between tests (e.g. a static collection or file) — make the test isolated
choices.feedback: The classic flake: tests sharing state under parallelism. Isolate or serialize.

choices.label: The CI machines are slower — increase all timeouts
choices.feedback: Slower machines expose timing assumptions; blanket timeout increases just move the flake.

choices.label: The test framework is buggy
choices.feedback: Blaming the framework is the last resort, not the first hypothesis.

simulations.debrief: Flaky tests get quarantined first (protect the signal), then root-caused — usually shared state under parallelism. Never rerun-until-green.

simulations.title: The appsettings that misfires
simulations.brief: EF Core can't find its connection string and logging is deaf. appsettings.json has 2 bugs in 12 lines.

sections.heading: C# Language
items: Value types — structs are value types: passing one to a method copies the entire value, so mutations hit the copy. Records are reference types with value-based equality synthesized by the compiler (Equals, GetHashCode, == all compare member values) — ideal for immutable…
Struct semantics — fixes: pass with ref/out, return the modified struct, or model it as a class (reference type) when identity and mutation matter.

Nullable — Nullable reference types (string? vs string) move nullability into the type system: the compiler warns when you dereference a maybe-null reference without checking. A plain class uses reference equality unless you override Equals/GetHashCode by hand.

Null safety — displayName documents the reality and forces callers to handle it (null check, ?. operator, or throw). try/catch for nulls and blanket string.Empty initialization hide the domain meaning of 'no display name'.
Task — unawaited tasks are fire-and-forget: Main doesn't wait for them, and exceptions in unobserved tasks surface unpredictably (or crash the process).
Common trap — records are reference types with reference equality.
Common trap — LINQ queries cache their results automatically after the first enumeration.
Common trap — the compiler caches struct field writes.
Common trap — using blocks are only for file I/O.

LINQ uses deferred execution — the query is just a definition until enumerated, and each enumeration re-executes it. Count() then foreach = two executions (two DB round-trips). Materialize once with ToList()/ToArray() when you need multiple passes, or restructure to a single enumeration.

items: Minimal APIs collapse the host setup — CreateBuilder configures DI/logging/config, Build() creates the app, MapGet maps a path to a handler delegate, Run() starts Kestrel.
Middleware runs in registration order — UseAuthentication builds the ClaimsPrincipal from the token/cookie; UseAuthorization then evaluates policies against that identity.

Eager loading — the decision is per query — eager where you know you'll need the data, not a global switch.
Include — Include(o => o.Customer) eager-loads via JOIN in the single initial query.

AsNoTracking — AsNoTracking() skips it, measurably speeding large read lists.

sections.heading: Deploy & Tooling
items: Dotnet — Dotnet build produces intermediate binaries assuming the SDK/tooling context; dotnet publish assembles the complete runnable deployment — app assemblies, NuGet dependencies, runtime config, static assets — into one folder.
Environments — one build, many environments — the twelve-factor pattern. #if directives fork the binary per environment; committed secrets leak to every clone.
Configuration — debug configuration disables optimizations, emits full debug symbols, and enables debug-only code paths — slower and heavier.

Kestrel — in production it typically sits behind a reverse proxy handling TLS termination, request filtering, and static files (defense in depth; Kestrel alone is fine but the proxy adds hardening). dotnet run is a development command, not a production host.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For C# Language: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one OOP & LINQ lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key ASP.NET Core terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
